evidence.correctness: Ran it. `python3.13 -m pytest -q tests` -> 6 passed. `PYTHONPATH=src python3.13 experiments/run.py` (45.6 s) reproduces experiments/results.txt byte-for-byte except the run-time line. Independent recomputes in my own scratchpad script (indep.py): (1) a brute-force enumeration of every 1-, 2- and 3-subset of sample-point candidates on 9 instances (n=40, rho=0.5, seeds 11-13) equals exact() on all 9; (2) coverage() of one size at the mean on 200,000 people matches the closed-form bivariate-normal box probability: rho=0 analytic (2*Phi(0.5)-1)^2 = 0.1466 vs 0.1479, rho=0.9 scipy multivariate_normal.cdf rectangle 0.2581 vs 0.2580; (3) a joint (not per-axis) brute-force search of the axis-aligned lattice gives 0.632/0.709 (rho 0.9, k 4/8) and 0.520/0.701 (rho 0, k 4/8) vs grid_run 0.628/0.711/0.514/0.698, so the per-axis window shortcut in _best_line costs under 0.6 points. The computations are right; the error is in a derived claim (README 80% count, see claims) and in the baseline choice (domain), not in the arithmetic.

evidence.craft: Read src/garment_sizeset/sizes.py, tests/test_sizeset.py, experiments/run.py, experiments/figure.py. Small, readable, vectorised numpy; MILP formulation (y_j, z_i, z_i <= sum C_ij y_j, sum y <= k) is the textbook max-coverage IP and returns HiGHS status, which run.py reports (all 54 solves proven optimal). Defects: grid_run places each axis from its marginal (_best_line) rather than jointly, harmless here (<0.6 pt, measured) but undocumented; the grid's offset search is a 9x9 loop calling coverage() each time (slow but fine at n=300); the exact candidate set is the sample itself, which the README states. No dead code, no silent fallbacks.
evidence.claims: Checked 6 README claims against results.txt and my reruns. Backed: the in-sample table (README.md:27-34) matches results.txt; greedy within 0 to 3.7 points of exact (max gap 3.7 at rho 0.9 k 6); held-out loss of 7 to 9 points (6.9 to 9.1). Not backed: (a) README.md:38 '6 for greedy and exact at rho 0.9' sizes needed for 80% - k=5 was never run (KS skips 5 and 7); I ran it: greedy 0.802, exact 0.836, so 5 suffices; (b) README.md:36 headline 'a regular grid is ... wasteful when they are tightly correlated' - true only of the axis-aligned lattice with step fixed at 2*tol; a regular graded run (bust and hip stepping together, the way real size runs are graded) with the same tolerance reaches 0.753 (k 4, 6 cm grade) and 0.899 (k 8, 4 cm grade) in-sample against exact 0.770/0.940 and lattice 0.628/0.711, and held-out 0.687 and 0.859 against exact 0.687 and 0.871, so the 'waste' is the lattice's orientation, not regularity; (c) sizes.py:65 calls the axis lattice 'the classic S M L size run', which is not how S-M-L runs are built; (d) README.md:3 'a new question' - optimal size-set choice as an integer program is a 1980s operations-research problem (Tryfos 1986) not cited. Limits and 'stylised, preliminary, synthetic' labels are present and honest.
evidence.fitness: A researcher building on this would first need prior work and a real population; neither is here. Nearest prior work: Tryfos (1986) 'An integer programming approach to the apparel sizing problem', J. Oper. Res. Soc. 37(10) - exactly this max-coverage/IP formulation; McCulloch, Paal & Ashdown (1998) 'An optimisation approach to apparel sizing', J. Oper. Res. Soc. 49(5) - optimising size locations with an aggregate-loss fit function on real anthropometry; Gupta & Gangadhar (2004) and later clustering-based sizing (k-means/aggregate loss) on national surveys (SizeUSA, ANSUR II). None is cited; the only reference is Nemhauser-Wolsey-Fisher 1978. The result is not new (greedy near-optimal for max coverage and non-grid sizes beating a lattice on correlated data are both known), the population is a synthetic bivariate normal with assumed parameters, and the main baseline is not the one practitioners use. As a teaching demo it is sound; as a step toward a paper it is a prototype.
evidence.domain: Compared against apparel sizing practice: ASTM D5585/D6240 body-measurement tables and ISO 8559-2 define size runs graded along a primary dimension, with secondary measurements stepping together (and sometimes drop/fit variants), i.e. a diagonal run in (bust, hip) space; ISO 8559-2 also names primary/secondary control dimensions and intervals. The subject's 'regular grid' is an axis-aligned r x c lattice, which no size standard uses, so the central finding compares the optimiser with a straw man; my graded-run baseline removes most of the gap (held-out within 0 to 1.2 points of exact at rho 0.9). Fit as a +-4 cm box in both measurements is a recognised simplification (accommodation box) but no aggregate-loss or ease model is considered, and two dimensions with equal sd and a 5 cm drop are assumed, not taken from ANSUR II or SizeUSA. A sizing researcher would not sign off on the method's conclusion.

defects.what: Headline 'a regular grid is wasteful when bust and hip are tightly correlated' rests on an axis-aligned r x c lattice that no size standard uses. A regular graded run (both measurements stepping together) closes most of the gap: rho 0.9 held-out 0.687/0.859 vs exact 0.687/0.871 (k 4/8), against lattice 0.596/0.677. The finding is about lattice orientation, not regularity.
'Sizes needed for 80%: 6 for greedy and exact at rho 0.9' - k=5 was never evaluated (KS = 1,2,3,4,6,8); at k=5 greedy fits 0.802 and exact 0.836, so 5 suffices.

Prior apparel-sizing optimisation not cited and novelty overstated ('a new question'): Tryfos 1986 (integer programming for apparel sizing, JORS 37(10)) and McCulloch, Paal & Ashdown 1998 (JORS 49(5)) solve this problem on real anthropometry; ASTM D5585/ISO 8559-2 define how runs are graded.

Tests cannot catch a broken greedy or grid: a greedy that ignores coverage (picks one size k times) and a lattice step of 3*tol both leave all 6 tests green; the 'greedy trap' test asserts only e >= g though greedy=0.875, exact=1.0 on that instance.
Docstring calls the axis-aligned lattice 'the classic S M L size run'; S-M-L runs are graded diagonally (all measurements step together).
Population is a synthetic bivariate normal with assumed means, sds and drop; no anthropometric survey (ANSUR II, SizeUSA) is used, so no number transfers to a real population (stated in Limitations).
README.md:37 lists greedy below grid only 'at k = 4 for rho 0 and 0.5'; results.txt also has greedy below grid at rho 0 k 6 (0.630 vs 0.640) and rho 0.5 k 1 (0.189 vs 0.197).

verdict: The code is small, correct and reproducible: exact() matches a brute-force enumeration on 9 instances, coverage() matches closed-form bivariate-normal box probabilities, and run.py and figure.py reproduce the committed results and SVG exactly. The research does not meet the bar. Its headline (a regular size grid wastes sizes when bust and hip are correlated) compares the optimiser with an axis-aligned lattice that no sizing standard uses; a regular graded run, the actual S-M-L practice, comes within 0 to 1.2 points of the exact optimum on held-out people at rho 0.9. The '6 sizes for 80%' claim skips k=5, where both methods already pass 80%. The optimal-size-set integer program is a 1986 operations-research result (Tryfos; McCulloch, Paal & Ashdown 1998), uncited, on a synthetic population. Two of three seeded core mutations survive the tests. Meets the bar: no (verification 1, claims 1, median 1). Finished for what it claims: yes.
